entities.name: Usama ibn Zayd
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Usama ibn Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi (died 678 CE) stands as a pivotal figure in early Islamic history, a companion and adopted grandson of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, whose unique lineage and military leadership profoundly shaped the nascent Muslim community. Born to Zayd ibn Haritha, one of the earliest converts to Islam and Muhammad's freedman and adopted son, and Umm Ayman, a freed Abyssinian slave who had served Muhammad's mother, Usama embodied the egalitarian principles of early Islam, rising to command despite his youth and diverse background. His life trajectory, from orphan to military commander, illustrates the meritocratic ideals championed during the foundational period of the Rashidun Caliphate.

Usama's most significant contribution was his appointment by Muhammad, shortly before the Prophet's death in 632 CE, to lead an expedition against the Byzantine Empire in Syria. This army, known as the Expedition of Usama, was tasked with avenging the Muslim defeat at the Battle of Mu'tah (629 CE) and securing the northern borders. Despite initial reluctance and even protests from some senior companions regarding Usama's youth (he was reportedly around 18-20 years old), Muhammad emphatically affirmed his command. Following Muhammad's death, the newly elected Caliph Abu Bakr faced immense pressure to recall the expedition amid growing apostasy movements (Ridda Wars) within Arabia, but he resolutely upheld Muhammad's final wish, dispatching Usama's army to Syria.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Usama ibn Zayd's leadership of the Syrian expedition in 632 CE was a critical test for the early Muslim community, affirming the authority of the first Caliph, Abu Bakr, and setting a precedent for military expansion that directly contributed to the later Islamic conquests of the Levant.
